clinicalPearls: The commonest form of scoliosis, presenting at or after ten years of age, and far more likely to progress to a significant curve in girls
The typical idiopathic pattern is a right thoracic curve, so a left thoracic curve is atypical and should prompt investigation for an underlying cause
The Adams forward-bend test reveals a rib hump from vertebral rotation, and a scoliometer quantifies the trunk rotation as a screening measure
The Cobb angle on a standing posteroanterior spinal radiograph defines curve magnitude and guides management thresholds
Remaining growth largely determines the risk of progression, so skeletal maturity is assessed using the Risser sign and other maturity indicators
It is a diagnosis of exclusion, made only after painful, rapidly progressive, neurologically abnormal, or atypical curves have been evaluated, often with magnetic resonance imaging

Management is stratified by curve size and growth remaining: observation for small curves, bracing to halt progression of moderate curves in the growing child, and surgery for large or progressive curves
reference.pathophysiology: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis is a three-dimensional structural deformity combining lateral curvature, axial vertebral rotation, and alteration of the normal sagittal profile, developing in an otherwise healthy adolescent without congenital or neuromuscular cause. Its aetiology is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with contributions from genetic predisposition and from disturbances of growth, neuromuscular control, connective tissue, and hormonal regulation during the adolescent growth spurt. Asymmetric growth of the vertebrae and the rapid spinal elongation of puberty allow curves to progress, and the vertebral rotation produces the rib prominence seen clinically. Because the label is idiopathic, structural, neurological, and syndromic causes must be excluded before the diagnosis is accepted.
additionalDifferentials: Neuromuscular scoliosis in cerebral palsy, spinal muscular atrophy, or muscular dystrophy
Scoliosis secondary to an intraspinal abnormality such as syrinx, tethered cord, or Chiari malformation
Syndromic scoliosis in neurofibromatosis, Marfan, or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Painful scoliosis from an osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma, or infection
Compensatory curve from leg-length discrepancy or a postural cause
additionalInvestigations: Standing posteroanterior and lateral whole-spine radiographs with Cobb angle measurement
Scoliometer trunk-rotation measurement during the Adams forward-bend test
Assessment of skeletal maturity using the Risser sign and other maturity markers
Whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging for atypical, painful, left thoracic, neurologically abnormal, or rapidly progressive curves
Thorough neurological examination including abdominal reflexes
Assessment for syndromic features and referral for genetic evaluation where indicated
redFlags: A left thoracic curve or other atypical pattern suggesting a non-idiopathic cause
Significant or persistent back pain, especially night pain
Neurological signs such as weakness, sensory change, gait disturbance, or asymmetric abdominal reflexes
Rapid progression, particularly during the growth spurt
Onset outside the expected age range or a large curve at first presentation
reference.prognosis: Most small curves remain stable and require only monitoring, and appropriately timed bracing can prevent progression in the growing child; large or neglected curves may progress into adulthood with cosmetic, and in severe cases cardiopulmonary, consequences, though surgical correction achieves durable deformity control.
pitfalls: Accepting an idiopathic label for an atypical, painful, or neurologically abnormal curve without imaging
Misjudging progression risk by not assessing remaining growth and skeletal maturity
Offering a brace after skeletal maturity, when it can no longer alter the curve
Underusing bracing in the growing child with a moderate progressive curve
Overlooking subtle neurological signs that indicate an intraspinal cause
management: Observe small curves with serial standing radiographs and Cobb-angle measurement through the remaining growth period
Prescribe a spinal orthosis (bracing) for moderate curves in the skeletally immature to prevent progression
Refer for posterior spinal fusion and instrumentation for large or progressive curves
Offer scoliosis-specific physiotherapy exercises as an adjunct
Track curve progression against skeletal maturity using the Risser sign and other maturity indicators
Investigate atypical, painful, left thoracic or neurologically abnormal curves with whole-spine MRI to exclude an underlying cause
Address the psychosocial and body-image impact as part of holistic care
